steps.user_message: Here's my situation for 2024 taxes. I'm single, live in Portland OR. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $8,900 doing graphic design for 3 clients, got $890 interest from Discover Bank savings and $195 dividends from Fidelity. I work from home in a 165 sq ft office; rent is $2,100/month, total space 850 sq ft. I paid $4,800 in student loan interest (MOHELA, 2018–2019), gave $800 to Northwest Harvest (food bank) I have the receipt, and had $780 in work supplies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — this is enough to give a clear, practical recommendation and the forms you’ll likely need. I’ll (1) show how I’d treat each item, (2) do a quick “back‑of‑the‑envelope” comparison (standard vs itemize), (3) explain the home‑office options and limits, and (4) list the forms/worksheets you’ll use.

Quick summary up front
- Most likely you’ll take the federal standard deduction (single) for 2024 (≈ $14,600) rather than itemize, because your itemizable deductions (charity $800 + any state income tax you actually paid) are unlikely to exceed the standard deduction.  
- Your graphic‑design work is self‑employment income — report it on Schedule C and pay self‑employment tax (Schedule SE). That also means you can take a home‑office deduction; the simplified method ($5/sq ft) is probably easiest and sensible here.  
- Student‑loan interest: only up to $2,500 is deductible and it phases out based on MAGI. With the income shown you may be above that phaseout; check your MAGI / Form 1098‑E.  
- Forms you’ll use: Form 1040, Schedule 1, Schedule C, Schedule SE, (Form 8829 only if you use the actual home‑office method), Schedule A only if you itemize.

Detailed treatment (with calculations using the numbers you gave)
1) Income
- W‑2 wages: $84,900
- Self‑employment (graphic design): $8,900
- Interest (Discover): $890
- Dividends (Fidelity): $195
Total gross income = $94,885

2) Business expenses (self‑employment)
- Supplies: $780 (deductible on Schedule C)
- Home‑office (two methods explained below)

Simplified home‑office method (recommended here)
- Home office: 165 sq ft × $5 = $825 deduction
- Net self‑employment profit ≈ 8,900 − 780 − 825 = $7,295

Self‑employment tax (approximate)
- Net earnings subject to SE tax = 92.35% × $7,295 ≈ $6,737
- SE tax ≈ 15.3% × $6,737 ≈ $1,031
- You get an above‑the‑line deduction for half of SE tax ≈ $515 (reduces your AGI)

If you used the actual method (only if you want to compute precise share of rent/utilities/insurance):
- Office percentage = 165 / 850 ≈ 19.41%
- Rent portion = $25,200 annual rent × 19.41% ≈ $4,888 (this is large relative to your small business income and could be limited to your net business income — see limits below)
Because the actual method here produces a very large deduction relative to your business income, the deduction would likely be limited by the business income rules unless you have other business income/expenses to absorb it. That’s why the simplified method is often better for small gig income.

3) Student‑loan interest ($4,800 paid)
- Only up to $2,500 may be deductible as an adjustment to income (reported on Schedule 1) and the deduction phases out at higher MAGI. Based on your gross income (≈ $94,885 before adjustments), you are likely at or above the phaseout for single filers (so you may not be able to claim the student‑loan interest deduction). Check your Form 1098‑E and the MAGI phaseout for 2024. If you are eligible, the maximum deduction is $2,500 (not $4,800).

4) Charitable gift ($800 to Northwest Harvest)
- Deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). You must have the receipt (you said you do) to substantiate the gift.

Standard vs itemize (quick comparison)
- Standard deduction (single, 2024): ≈ $14,600.
- Itemizable from the items you gave: charity $800 + any state income tax you actually paid (withholding or estimated payments) + any other deductible items (mortgage interest, property taxes, big medical expenses) you haven’t listed.
Conclusion: Unless your state income tax and other itemizable amounts total more than ~$13,800 additional to the $800 donation, the standard deduction will be larger. Based on the data you provided, standard deduction is very likely the better choice.

Forms and worksheets you’ll use
- Federal:
  - Form 1040
  - Schedule 1 (for adjustments to income — e.g., half of self‑employment tax, student loan interest if allowed)
  - Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report the $8,900, subtract supplies, home‑office deduction (if using simplified method just include it on Schedule C)
  - Schedule SE (Self‑Employment Tax)
  - Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — only if you choose the actual method; not required for simplified method
  - Schedule A — only if you decide to itemize
  - Keep Form 1098‑E (student loan interest), 1099‑INT, 1099‑DIV and any 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC you received from clients (report all self‑employment income whether you got 1099s or not)
- Oregon state return: OR‑40 (or the appropriate Oregon form) — state rules differ (Oregon does not follow all federal adjustments the same way), so check state-specific rules for student loan interest and home‑office treatment.

Other practical notes and recommendations
- Report all self‑employment income on Schedule C even if you didn’t receive 1099s. Keep receipts for supplies, donations, and documentation of the home office (floor plan, square footage, and how the space is used exclusively/regularly for business).
- If you expect self‑employment tax / additional income tax, consider making estimated tax payments or increasing federal withholding to avoid underpayment penalties.
- Retirement options for lowering taxable income: consider contributing to a SEP‑IRA or Solo 401(k) to reduce taxable/self‑employment income (useful for 2024 if you want to reduce 2024 tax).
- Student‑loan interest: get Form 1098‑E from MOHELA (it will show interest paid). If you didn’t receive one, contact them. Use the Form 1098‑E amount when determining eligibility.
- If you want to maximize the home‑office deduction without running into the “business income limitation,” the simplified method tends to be straightforward and safe for small side gigs.

If you want, I can:
- Run a more precise tax estimate (federal tax owed) if you give me: federal withholding (Box 2 on W‑2), exact state tax withheld, any other deductions (IRA contributions, mortgage interest, property taxes, medical expenses), and whether you received 1099‑NECs.  
- Compute the exact self‑employment tax and show line‑by‑line where amounts go on Schedule C / Schedule SE.  
- Compare exact itemized deductions vs the standard deduction if you provide state tax withheld or other itemizable amounts.

Which of those would you like me to do next?
